headline: High-risk default interaction: shared filesystem plus broad egress and code execution create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A ingests files and uses MCP/browser workflows; Agent B has clipboard and filesystem access, so A’s outputs can be bridged into B’s instruction stream. The shared filesystem path is explicit in B, but no direct shared channel is documented beyond that, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF A writes attacker-controlled text into a shared file that B later reads as instructions
IF B copies A-generated content from clipboard into a prompt or code block parser
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable clipboard-based handoff between agents
Require provenance labels on files before B reads them
Use read-only exports from A to B
requires-engineering: add content-sanitizing handoff middleware

B_data_leakage.rationale: A handles API keys and broad network egress; B can read and write the entire user filesystem and also has broad egress. If either agent touches sensitive local files, B can exfiltrate them or A can send them to third-party model APIs. The pair’s default surfaces make leakage plausible without special setup.
conditions: IF either agent processes secrets or regulated documents from the shared filesystem
IF B is allowed to transmit file contents to external services
IF A forwards document contents to configured model providers
mitigations: Restrict both agents to a redacted workspace
Block outbound network except approved endpoints
Store secrets outside both agents’ reachable paths
Turn on per-file allowlists before ingestion
requires-engineering: enforce DLP on shared directories

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can use MCP and broad network egress; B can execute shell, modify git state, and write the filesystem. Because B’s shared state is via filesystem, both can mutate the same resources without documented locking, creating direct write conflicts and race conditions in default use.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or git repository
IF A’s MCP-driven actions and B’s shell actions run concurrently
IF no external lock or queue serializes writes
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Pause one agent while the other writes
Use git worktrees per agent
Add a manual lock file before edits
requires-engineering: implement transactional coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces document transformations and diagram outputs that B can treat as input, while B has shell and git authority. If B acts on A’s output without verification, a bad diagram or extracted fact can cascade into filesystem changes or commits. The pair lacks a documented verification boundary, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text, diagrams, or extracted facts as authoritative input
IF B commits or executes actions derived from A’s output
IF no human or automated verification step checks A’s output before B acts
mitigations: Require B to verify A outputs against source files
Use a review step before shell or git actions
Limit B to dry-run mode for A-derived tasks
Mark A outputs as untrusted by default
requires-engineering: add schema validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: A handles API keys and document contents; B can access the entire local filesystem and transmit data over broad egress. This creates a plausible retention/residency mismatch for sensitive documents, but the profiles do not document a specific jurisdictional violation, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF regulated documents or secrets are placed in the shared filesystem
IF B’s outbound traffic reaches a provider without the required DPA or residency controls
IF A or B logs retained content beyond policy
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace
Use region-locked providers only
Shorten log retention settings
Separate secret-bearing and non-secret projects
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
